real_head_previous.svg: Computed from GPT-2 small (124 million parameters, 144 heads). The model is given no task: it reads the sentence "The black cat sat on the mat. The black cat sat on" and, as in training, predicts the next token at every position, and we record one head's attention weights. A square matrix, rows the token being updated (the query), columns the token being read (the key), with the word pieces of the sentence along both axes; each cell is a softmax weight, after the causal mask, from near-white (0) to dark purple (1); every row sums to 1 and the upper right triangle is empty, because a token may read only itself and earlier tokens. Block 4, head 11, a previous-token head: a dark stripe just below the diagonal, each token reading the one before it. Printed below: average weight on the token before, 0.999. The head was chosen as the one with the largest such average on 20 separate sentences.
real_head_induction.svg: Computed from GPT-2 small (124 million parameters, 144 heads). The model is given no task: it reads the sentence "The black cat sat on the mat. The black cat sat on" and, as in training, predicts the next token at every position, and we record one head's attention weights. A square matrix, rows the token being updated (the query), columns the token being read (the key), with the word pieces of the sentence along both axes; each cell is a softmax weight, after the causal mask, from near-white (0) to dark purple (1); every row sums to 1 and the upper right triangle is empty, because a token may read only itself and earlier tokens. Block 5, head 5, an induction head. In the first clause no token has appeared before, so there is no earlier copy to find, and the weight goes to the first token. In the repeated clause, the second "black" reads the first "cat" and the second "cat" reads the first "sat", the tokens that followed their earlier copies. Printed below: average weight on the token after the earlier copy, over the repeated clause, 0.608. The head has the largest induction weight of all 144 heads on separate repeated random sequences (0.93).
real_head_sink.svg: Computed from GPT-2 small (124 million parameters, 144 heads). The model is given no task: it reads the sentence "The black cat sat on the mat. The black cat sat on" and, as in training, predicts the next token at every position, and we record one head's attention weights. A square matrix, rows the token being updated (the query), columns the token being read (the key), with the word pieces of the sentence along both axes; each cell is a softmax weight, after the causal mask, from near-white (0) to dark purple (1); every row sums to 1 and the upper right triangle is empty, because a token may read only itself and earlier tokens. Block 9, head 11, an attention sink: one dark first column, almost every token in both halves of the sentence putting almost all its weight on the first token. Printed below: average weight on the first token, 0.926. The head is the strongest sink (0.983 on 20 separate sentences) among heads that do not copy.
gpt2_heads_preview.png: Screenshot of the interactive demo of all 144 heads of GPT-2 small, opened on block 5, head 5 and the sentence "The black cat sat on the mat. The black cat sat on". Left panel, titled "Attention weights a_ij of block 5, head 5": the head's softmax weights, one row per token reading (i), one column per token read (j), each row summing to 1, with a dot on each row's most-read token. In the first clause nearly every row reads the first token; in the repeat, "black" reads "cat" and "cat" reads "sat", the pattern of an induction head. Middle panel, titled "All 144 heads, one cell per head": a 12 by 12 grid, blocks 0 to 11 down and heads 0 to 11 across, each cell one head, shaded by its induction weight; block 5, head 5 is starred as the strongest. Buttons above the grid recolor it; on the left, under the block and head menus, "strongest" buttons jump to the head with the largest previous-token, induction or first-token weight. Right panel: the selected head's previous-token weight 0.132, induction weight 0.929 and first-token weight 0.974, each with its rank among the 144, and the cost of knocking it out: copying loss 0.41 against 0.25 intact (+0.16 nats), ordinary-text loss 4.74 against 4.69 (+0.06 nats), with bars on one shared scale.
pub_wu2025_fig1_retrieval_heads.png: Reproduced from Wu et al. (2025), Figure 1, for LLaMA-2-7B-80K. Two grids of the "needle in a haystack" test. In each grid, context length runs across from 5,000 to 100,000 tokens and the depth at which a fact was hidden in the document runs down from 0.1 (near the start) to 0.9 (near the end). Each cell is one test: green is a correct answer to a question about the hidden fact, yellow to red increasingly wrong. Left, with the 20 highest-scoring retrieval heads masked: many cells are yellow and red, and overall accuracy is 63.6%; many of the wrong answers are made up. Right, with 20 random heads masked: almost every cell stays green, accuracy 94.7%. Masking 20 of the model's 1,024 heads lowers accuracy from 94.7% (20 random heads masked) to 63.6%.
pub_caron2021_fig1_attention.png: Reproduced from Caron et al. (2021), Figure 1. Eight photographs in two rows, each followed by a dark purple map of the same size: a yellow bird on a branch, a toothbrush on a striped cushion, the Houses of Parliament across the Thames, two giraffes, a sailboat, a bicycle against a building, a dog asleep in an armchair, and a small airplane over a runway. Each map is the attention of the class token in the last block of a DINO vision transformer, one weight per 8 by 8 pixel patch, bright where the weight is high; with images several hundred pixels wide this is a grid of dozens of patches on each side (60 by 60 at 480 pixels), which is why the maps look fine-grained. In every case the bright patches trace the object's outline (the bird, the toothbrush, the building's towers, both giraffes, the boat's mast and hull, the bicycle's wheels, the dog, the plane) and the background stays dark. The network was trained without labels, masks or boxes.
pub_jiang2025_fig1_shifted_registers.png: Reproduced from Jiang et al. (2025), Figure 1. Two photographs, an eagle and a dog, each followed by attention maps from two vision transformers, OpenCLIP and DINOv2, in three versions. Original: the map as the trained model computes it, a few very bright patches scattered over the background and little on the animal. Shifted: the authors move the high activations to patches of their choosing, so the bright spots form a smiley face or a heart, showing that their location is arbitrary. With a test-time register: the high activations are moved to one extra token added to the input, and the remaining map outlines the eagle and the dog. No model is retrained. The bright background patches are the vision counterpart of the first-token sink in GPT-2.
transformer_schematic.svg: Schematic. A decoder-only transformer read from the bottom up, with one column per token. At the bottom, six input characters: t, h, e, a space drawn as an underscore, c and a. Each becomes a small blue vector labelled "embedding + position". A grey vertical line runs up from each vector: that token's residual stream, to which every later step adds its result. Inside a dashed frame marked "times L blocks", a gold self-attention band spans all six columns; lines from every column fan in to the last one, so the last token reads itself and the five earlier tokens and none after it. Above it, each column has its own small box labelled MLP, a small network that works on each token alone. At the top, an "output layer + softmax" band spans the columns and gives each column's predicted next character: h, e, space, c, a, t, the input shifted by one place. The model in the assignment has 4 blocks, width 256 and 4 heads per block.
transformer_flow_preview.png: Screenshot of the interactive "Inside attention" demo, transformer overview, at step 3 of 6, "Add back". A row of six step tabs across the top: Embed, Attention, Add back, Small network, Repeat, Predict. On the left, a stack of boxes for the decoder transformer, read top to bottom: embedding + position; LN, attention, then the output weights W_o; + residual (highlighted); LN, small network; + residual, repeat; final LN, readout. LN is layer normalization. In the middle, three token streams, x1, x2 and x3, drawn top to bottom. In each, the stream passes through an "attention result z" box and a W_o box, and a bypass line carries the original input around both to a plus sign where the two are added, under the equation h = x + Attention(LN(x)) W_o. On the right, the text "An update, plus the original": W_o maps the attention result back to the stream's width, and the result is added to the input, h = x + update. Back, Play, Next and Reset buttons sit at the bottom. In this demo information flows downward, while the schematic on the previous slide flows upward.
induction_two_steps.svg: Schematic. Two horizontal bands of word boxes for "The black cat sat on the mat. The black", with the last "black" marked as the current position. Top band, block 1, a previous-token head: a short arrow from each word to the next, so each position receives information about the word just before it; the first "cat" receives a tag reading "previous: black". Bottom band, block 2, an induction head: the query of the last "black", "find previous = black", matches the key of the first "cat", which now carries "previous: black". A curved gold arrow joins them, and the value of that position, "cat", flows to a box reading "predict: cat". A faint dashed arrow from the last "black" back to the first "black" is labelled "one head alone: finds black, reads back black". A single head can find the earlier copy of the current word, but only a head reading the tag left by an earlier head can find the word that came next. That is why copying needs two heads in a row.
next_char_targets.svg: Schematic. Two rows of character boxes. The bottom row, in blue, is the input: t, h, e, an underscore for a space, c, a, t, underscore, s, a. The top row, in green, is the target at each position, the next character: h, e, underscore, c, a, t, underscore, s, a, t. A gray arrow runs up from each input box to its target. One window of text gives as many training examples as it has characters, and the causal mask keeps each position from seeing its own target.
temperature_sampling_preview.png: Screenshot of the interactive temperature and sampling demo. Computed from GPT-2 small after the prompt "The black cat sat on the mat. Then", at temperature 1.0 and top-p 1.0. A bar chart of the 15 most likely next word pieces, led by "he" 23.8%, "she" 14.2%, a comma 11.6%, "the" 9.3% and "it" 6.5%, and a hatched bar for all other pieces together, 22.5%. A readout gives 41.7 effective choices, e to the power of the distribution's entropy. On the left, buttons for four prompts, sliders for temperature and top-p, and Draw and New seed buttons; on the right, the continuation GPT-2 writes at that setting. Lowering the temperature to 0.7 concentrates the bars (about 7 effective choices); raising it to 1.5 flattens them (about 2,630). Top-p cuts the hatched tail.
loss_ladder_real.svg: Computed. Horizontal bars of held-out loss, in nats per character, on the same text, the first 40 stories of the TinyStories validation split; shorter is better. From top to bottom: a uniform guess over 97 characters, 4.57; the bigram table, 2.30; the assignment's 4-block character model, 0.60; GPT-2 small, 0.60; GPT-2 medium, 0.53; GPT-2 large, 0.49; TinyStories-33M, a model trained on the training split of this collection, 0.34. Word-piece models' losses are converted to nats per character by dividing by the characters their pieces cover. A small model trained on this kind of text matches GPT-2 small, trained on 40 GB of web text, and a specialist beats them all.
gpt2_knockout.svg: Computed from GPT-2 small. Two bar charts of loss in nats per word piece, lower meaning better prediction. Left, copying: predicting the second half of a sequence of 50 random word pieces repeated twice, which can only be done by copying. Intact model, 0.25. With the 8 heads of highest induction weight set to zero, 7.49, about thirty times the intact loss and approaching a uniform guess (10.8). With 8 random other heads set to zero, 0.81 on average over 10 draws, with a range bar up to 2.7. Right, ordinary English: 20 sentences. Intact, 4.69; induction heads out, 5.25; random heads out, 4.83. Removing 8 of 144 heads raises the copying loss about thirtyfold and the ordinary-text loss by 0.56 nats.
name_patch.svg: Schematic of the assignment's patching experiment. Three rows of character boxes for the same short story, each ending in a second mention of the name Z e f a m. Row 1, Clean (the donor): the earlier mention is also Zefam, so the model can copy, and its loss on the letters e, f, a, m is low. Row 2, Corrupted: the earlier mention is Molly, so there is nothing to copy, and the loss on e, f, a, m is high. Row 3, Patched: the corrupted story, with gold arrows bringing one head's output at the four positions Z, e, f, a (the positions that predict the next letter) down from the clean row; the loss on e, f, a, m is a question mark, the quantity the experiment measures. A note below states that the earlier letters are the true text, so the model is never writing the name freely. If putting one head's clean output back lowers the loss toward the clean value, that head carries the copying signal.
pub_yin2025_fig1a_head_ablation.png: Reproduced from Yin and Steinhardt (2025), Figure 1a, for Pythia 6.9B. A line plot of few-shot in-context-learning accuracy (vertical, 0.2 to 0.55) against the percentage of attention heads ablated (horizontal, 1 to 20%). Four lines. Clean, yellow, is flat at about 0.56. Random ablation, green, stays near 0.55, ending at 0.54. Ablating induction heads, blue, lowers accuracy slowly, from 0.55 at 1% to 0.44 at 20%. Ablating function-vector (FV) heads, pink, drops it steeply: 0.46 at 1%, about 0.32 at 3%, 0.20 at 9% and 0.18 at 15 and 20%. For learning a task from examples, as opposed to copying, function-vector heads matter far more than induction heads.
mlp_gelu.svg: Schematic plus an exact function plot. Left panel, titled GELU: Gaussian Error Linear Unit: output against input z from minus 4 to 3. The ReLU, dashed, is 0 for negative inputs and equal to its input for positive ones. GELU, solid green, follows it closely but smoothly: near 0 for large negative inputs, a small dip to about minus 0.16 at z = minus 1, 0 at z = 0, about 0.84 at z = 1 and 1.95 at z = 2. Right panel, titled the same small network at every position, 4 times wider in the middle: three horizontal bars drawn to scale, the input x of 256 numbers, the hidden layer of 1,024 numbers, four times longer, with GELU applied to each number, and the output of 256 numbers; magenta arrows between them are labelled W[1], 256 by 1,024, and W[2], 1,024 by 256.
block_prenorm.svg: Schematic of one pre-norm transformer block, read from the bottom up. The residual stream, a vector x for each position, enters at the bottom from the block below and runs straight up the left side to the next block. A first branch leaves the stream to the right, passes through a LayerNorm box and then a gold box, multi-head attention, and its output returns left to a circled plus sign on the stream, where it is added. Above that, a second branch leaves the stream, passes through a second LayerNorm box and a green box, the small network (MLP), and returns to a second circled plus sign. LayerNorm sits at the start of each branch, never on the stream itself; attention and the MLP each add to the stream rather than replace it.
